MosoFin · three-way match, in plain words

Should this bill be paid?

Before money goes out, three documents should agree: what you ordered, what arrived, and what the supplier billed. This skill checks that they do, line by line, and tells you what to pay, what to hold, and what to send back.

The 20-second version

You give it the purchase order, the delivery record and the invoice, or let it read them from your books. It compares price, quantity and item on every line, applies your tolerance, and lists every difference with a reason and an owner. Then it recommends Pay, Hold or Reject. It never pays anything itself.

Three documents, one question

Ordered, arrived, billed: do they agree?

A purchase order says what you agreed to buy and at what price. A goods receipt says what actually turned up. The invoice says what the supplier wants paid. Each one is written by a different person at a different time, which is exactly why comparing them catches so much. The US government will not pay a supplier without a receiving report to back the invoice1; this skill applies the same discipline to a small business.

The mistake it catches

A PO number on the invoice is not a match

Suppliers print your purchase-order number on their invoices as a courtesy. In many offices that is enough: the number is there, the invoice is approved, the invoice is paid. But a printed number checks nothing until someone compares it with the order. The skill opens the order the number points to and compares the two.

Most differences the skill finds are honest ones: a price list changed, a delivery was short, an invoice arrived twice. It reports what it sees as amounts and counts, never as an accusation. People decide what it means.

One honest limit

It can only match the documents you actually have

The invoice is always in your books. The purchase order often is: in QuickBooks Online, purchase orders exist only on the Plus and Advanced plans, and a PO is closed when it's added to a bill3. The delivery record usually isn't: receiving happens in a warehouse, on a clipboard, or nowhere. So the first thing the skill does is count the legs it has.

With all three it runs a three-way match. With orders and invoices but no delivery records it runs a two-way match and says so, in the report and in the file name, because the missing leg is the one that proves the goods arrived, and the five tests that depend on it did not run. Without that line, a test that never ran would look like one that passed.

How a run starts

It asks six questions before it looks at anything

  1. Use your MosoFin connection, or upload the files yourself?
    Either works. You don't need a subscription to use it.
  2. How much difference is acceptable on price, on quantity, on the total?
    Your policy, not the skill's. If you don't give one, it expects an exact match and flags every penny.
  3. Who may approve an order, and up to what amount?
    A perfectly matching invoice on an unapproved order is still unauthorised spending.
  4. Do you buy services as well as goods? What stands in for a delivery record?
    A signed "work completed" note plays the receipt's part.
  5. Any orders in a foreign currency, and how do you convert them?
    A price difference that is really an exchange-rate move is the classic false alarm.
  6. Who sorts out the exceptions?
    Every difference gets a named owner, not a pile.

Then it reads your answers back: "Matching September's invoices for Northbrook Trading against purchase orders and goods receipts, 2% price tolerance, exact on quantity. Go ahead?" It waits for your yes.

What you get back

Pay, hold or reject, and why, line by line

A recommendation per invoicePay, Hold or Reject, with the matched amount and the disputed amount. A person acts on it.
Every line, side by sideOrdered, received and billed quantities; ordered and billed prices; the difference; the tolerance applied; and how the line was matched.
Every exception, with an ownerFifteen kinds, from price creep to a damaged delivery billed in full to an order nobody approved, each with a severity and a next step.
What only the whole month showsA supplier always just inside tolerance; receipts posted in bulk on one date; goods received but never billed, which you owe for and should book4.
What it never does
  • Never pays, holds or releases money. It recommends; a person acts.
  • Never invents a tolerance. How much overbilling is acceptable is your decision.
  • Never lets a test that couldn't run look like a pass. It lists what it couldn't check, and why.
  • Never concludes fraud. It reports patterns with amounts and counts; people conclude.
  • Never changes your books, and never reads anything before you say yes.
Words you'll hear

Six terms, in plain English

Purchase order (PO)
Your written order to a supplier: what, how many, at what price. In QuickBooks Online it's a Plus or Advanced feature, closed when it becomes a bill3.
Goods receipt
The record of what arrived: how many, and in what condition. Government buyers call it a receiving report, and won't pay without one1.
Tolerance
The difference you're willing to accept without a question, say 2% on price. The skill applies yours; without one it expects an exact match.
Received, not billed
Goods that arrived but the invoice hasn't. You already owe for them: accounting standards treat an obligation you can't avoid, arising from something that already happened, as a liability4.
Override
Paying an invoice despite an exception. Fine with a written reason and a named approver; a pile of unexplained overrides is the control switched off.
Separation of duties
The person who orders shouldn't also receive, approve and pay. Splitting authority, custody and record-keeping is the basic control against fraud and error5; the skill flags one name across several steps.
Sources

Where the facts on this page come from

Government procurement rules, the US internal-control standard, the fraud examiners' association, an accounting standard-setter and the software's own documentation, as published when checked on 21 October 2026. Follow the link for today's wording. What the skill does comes from the skill's own file.

  1. Federal Acquisition Regulation 32.905: Payment documentation and processInvoice payments must be supported by a receiving report or other authorisation showing quantities received and accepted; a proper invoice carries the order number, description, quantity, unit price and extended price.
  2. ACFE: Occupational Fraud 2024: A Report to the Nations, key findings1,921 cases; billing schemes in 22% of cases with a $100,000 median loss, the most common asset-misappropriation scheme; 32% of frauds occurred where internal controls were lacking.
  3. Intuit: Create and send purchase orders in QuickBooks OnlinePurchase orders are available on the Plus and Advanced plans; a PO is Open until added to a bill or expense, then Closed. The article does not cover recording goods received.
  4. IFRS Foundation: Conceptual Framework for Financial Reporting, project summary (2018)A liability is a present obligation to transfer an economic resource as a result of past events; an obligation is a duty the entity has no practical ability to avoid.
  5. GAO: Standards for Internal Control in the Federal Government (Green Book), GAO-25-107721, ¶10.21–10.23Segregate authority, custody and accounting; where that is not practical, design alternative controls.

Not backed by an outside authority: the fifteen exception types, their severities and the "exact match if no tolerance is given" default are the skill's own rules. They are sound accounts-payable practice, not a published standard.
